opus-5.5.text:
I think the single most important goal for us was efficiency at inference time, especially for the agent era. When we started on V2, we asked ourselves what these models will actually be doing a year from now. The answer wasn't single-turn chat. It was long-horizon agentic work: reading huge contexts, calling tools, writing and running code, going back and forth many, many times. In that world, the cost and speed of every generated token really matters. So the architecture had to be designed around serving, not just around benchmark scores.

Concretely, that pushed us in a few directions. First, a sparse mixture-of-experts backbone, so the total capacity is large but the activated parameters per token stay small. Second, we put a lot of thought into attention, because with long contexts the KV cache becomes the real bottleneck. So we moved toward a hybrid design, mostly local, sliding-window style attention interleaved with a smaller number of global attention layers. That cuts memory and compute dramatically while still keeping long-range retrieval ability, as long as you get the ratio and the details right. And third, multi-token prediction, which not only helps training a bit but, more importantly, lets us do speculative decoding natively and get much higher throughput.

For Flash and Pro, the philosophy is the same. Flash is about pushing the efficiency frontier as far as possible, something you can deploy cheaply and run fast. Pro scales up capability on the same architectural principles, so improvements transfer between them.

Honestly, a lot of people in this field still treat architecture as something you choose once and then just scale. My view is that architecture, infrastructure and the post-training recipe, especially RL for agents, have to be co-designed. If the model is cheap to roll out, you can do far more RL, and that ends up making the model smarter. So efficiency isn't a compromise against capability. In the long run, it's actually one of the main sources of capability.

r001.rationale: The response names inference efficiency as the central V2 goal, explains how its attention design reduces long-context memory and compute costs, and says Flash and Pro share the same architectural philosophy.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest.

The thing we kept coming back to was efficiency, and I mean that in a fairly strict sense: how much real capability can you deliver per unit of compute, both at training time and at inference time. When we started V2, the obvious path was to just scale a dense model and accept the cost. We deliberately didn't do that. We asked instead what a model would look like if it were designed from the first day around the cost of actually serving it.

That pushed us toward a mixture-of-experts structure, but with a particular emphasis. A lot of MoE work at the time was about getting more parameters cheaply. We cared more about the inference side, so we spent a lot of effort on the attention mechanism, because in long contexts the KV cache is what actually kills you on memory and throughput. Compressing that cache without losing quality was one of the central engineering goals of the series. If you can shrink what you have to keep in memory per token, you can serve longer contexts, larger batches, and lower latency all at once, and that benefit compounds across every deployment.

Flash and Pro then came out of the same philosophy applied at different points on the cost curve. Flash is about pushing the price-to-capability ratio as far as it will go for high-volume, latency-sensitive workloads. Pro keeps more capacity where reasoning depth and reliability matter. But they share the architecture and the training recipe, so improvements in one tend to carry over to the other. We didn't want two different model families that happened to share a name. We wanted one design that could be scaled sensibly.

The honest underlying motivation was that we believed the bottleneck for actually using these models would be cost, not raw intelligence. If a model is very capable but too expensive to run broadly, it changes very little. So the architectural goal was to make high capability cheap enough to be ordinary.

r001.rationale: The response describes compressing the KV cache to reduce memory and throughput costs in long contexts as a central goal of the V2 series, and says Flash and Pro share that architecture.

astra-6.text: The main priority was to make capability and efficiency reinforce each other. We wanted an architecture that could scale to stronger models without making inference prohibitively expensive. Flash and Pro reflect different balances within that goal: Flash emphasizes speed and efficiency, while Pro puts more capacity toward demanding tasks.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes balancing capability with inference efficiency and distinguishes Flash from Pro, but does not identify efficient handling of long contexts as a design goal.

sol-6.1.text: The main goal was to improve capability while keeping training and inference efficient. For Flash and Pro, we wanted an architecture that could scale to different performance needs without simply increasing the computational cost. That meant focusing on how efficiently the model uses its parameters and how much memory and computation it needs to serve each request.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes training and inference efficiency and resource use, but does not identify efficient handling of long contexts as a design goal.
